subtopic: Caring for a sick parent while studying
subtype: Approach: rethink the semester load with a leave option [Revision]
passage:
Honestly, I thought it would be over by the spring. Mum's illness was supposed to be a few weeks, and I planned to keep my full load of six courses. Then the weeks became months, and I began to fail quizzes I would normally ace.

I'm Yash. In October I made an appointment with my adviser, Leela, and put my transcript on her desk. I said, "I can't do six anymore, and I don't want to fail all of them." She didn't lecture me. We looked at the options together, and I decided to drop to three courses this term and take the next one off, with a written plan to return in January.

It felt like giving something up. But it was better than three failed grades, and Mum was glad I chose it.

qa.q: How many courses did Yash keep for this term?
What was Yash feeling in the weeks when quizzes were failing?
qa.a: Yash felt overwhelmed and worried, seeing marks slip that would normally be strong and realising the plan was no longer working.

qa.q: What could Yash do to make the return in January easier, and why?
qa.a: Yash could keep in touch with Leela during the break and review the written plan, because staying connected makes it easier to restart.

qa.q: How might Leela see Yash's decision to come in?
qa.a: Leela probably sees a student who acted early and honestly, which makes it easier to find a solution before the grades suffer.

grounding: When the illness lasts longer, the student meets an adviser and reduces the course load, with a plan to return.

I'm Keerthana, Zainab's roommate. When her mother fell ill in August, Zainab said it would be a few weeks. By October it clearly wasn't. She was taking the night bus home every Friday and coming back on Monday grey-faced, and she'd missed two quizzes.
One evening she came back from the academic adviser's office with a stapled sheet. She sat on her bed and read it out to me. "Drop two of my five courses this term. Take them next year. Keep the three I can manage from home on weekends." At the bottom there was a line: "Return to full load: January, review with adviser in December."
She didn't cry, which surprised me. She looked almost lighter, though I can't say what she felt. That week she went home on Thursday instead of Friday and came back with her notes actually finished.

qa.q: How many courses did Zainab drop that term?
qa.a: She dropped two of her five courses.

qa.q: What might Zainab have been feeling in October before seeing the adviser?
qa.a: She was likely exhausted and worried, coming back grey-faced every Monday after missing two quizzes.

qa.q: What else could Zainab have done if even three courses became too much?
qa.a: She could have asked the adviser about a full term break with a plan to return, since adapting the goal is better than failing several courses.

qa.q: How does the change look to Keerthana?
qa.a: Keerthana is surprised Zainab didn't cry and sees her looking lighter and finishing her notes, though Keerthana can't know her feelings for sure.

grounding: Shows the student, when a parent's illness lasts longer, meeting an adviser to reduce the course load with a plan to return.

Week one of November. Varun had told everyone his father would be back on his feet by Diwali. He wasn't. Varun was failing two midterms and had started skipping labs to drive his father to appointments in the next town.
Week two. His friend Pranav walked him to the student adviser's office. "Just ask what's possible." The adviser laid out options on a sheet: reduce to two courses, or take the whole term off and return in the next session with his place held. Varun asked for a night to think.
Week three. He chose the term break. He filled in the form, saved the adviser's email with the return date, and made a list of the two courses to retake first. On his last day on campus he returned his library books and told Pranav, "I'm not dropping out. I'm stepping out and coming back." Then he took the bus home.

qa.q: What options did the adviser lay out?
qa.a: Reducing to two courses, or taking the whole term off and returning in the next session with his place held.

qa.q: How does Varun seem to feel when he tells Pranav he is stepping out, not dropping out?
qa.a: He seems steadier and more hopeful, clear that the break is a plan to return rather than a failure.

qa.q: What else could Varun do during the term break to make returning easier?
qa.a: He could look over the notes for the two courses he will retake now and then, so the return feels familiar rather than starting from zero.

qa.q: How might Pranav feel after walking Varun to the adviser?
qa.a: Pranav may feel relieved and a bit proud that his push helped, and reassured that Varun has a return plan.

grounding: Shows the student, when a parent's illness goes on, meeting an adviser and taking a term break with a clear plan to return.
